objectives: Name the three parts of the story.
Tell who Mai meets in the forest.
Say what a cub, a bramble and a fox are.
Follow the steps Mai used to help the fox cub.
Explain why the forest talked to Mai.
Tell the story to someone else in your own words.

sections.body:
This is a story about a girl called Mai. Mai is seven years old. She likes small things: pebbles, buttons, and birds with clever names.

Every good story has three parts. It has a beginning, a middle and an end. The beginning tells you who the story is about. The middle is where something goes wrong. The end is where everything comes right again.

Mai's story begins at the edge of a forest. The forest is called the Whispering Wood. Its trees are old and its path is soft with leaves.

The middle is the strange part. Mai hears a small voice crying in the brambles. When she helps, the animals of the wood begin to speak out loud. An owl speaks. A fox speaks. A deer speaks.

And the end is the best part of all. Mai walks home through the trees, and she is not alone.

This story has one rule inside it. The forest only speaks to people who stop and listen. Remember that rule, because it is the whole surprise of the story.
examples: This is the beginning of Mai's story.
The middle is the part where the animals speak.
The end is the part where Mai walks home.
sections.heading: A forest where the animals talk

sections.body:
Mai went for a walk on a warm afternoon. She took a basket, a bread roll and a red ball.

She left the path. She wanted to see what was behind the big green ferns. She pushed the branches aside and looked.

A voice came out of the thicket. It was small and it was crying.

"Please," said the voice. "Please help me. My leg is stuck."

Mai could not see anybody. Then she looked down, low down, near the roots. There was a little fox cub with one back leg caught in the brambles. The brambles are thorny branches that grow together and hold on tight.

The cub's fur was brown and orange, and his eyes were very big. He was trying to pull away, and every pull made the thorns tighter.

"Do not pull," said Mai. "Pulling makes it worse. I will cut them."

Mai took out her small bread knife. She did not cut quickly. She cut one thorn at a time, and she spoke to him the whole time, so he would not be afraid.
examples: Please help me. My leg is stuck.
Do not pull. Pulling makes it worse.
I will cut them, one at a time.
sections.heading: The cry behind the brambles

sections.body:
At last the last thorn came loose. The cub shook himself and sat down.

"Thank you," he said. "My name is Rusty. And you are the first person who has ever helped me and then stayed to talk."

Mai blinked. The fox had spoken words. Not barks. Words.

Then a voice came down from above.

"She listened," said the owl on the branch. The owl was very old and very round. "That is why she can hear us."

"The wood speaks to everyone," said Rusty. "But the wood only speaks to a person who stops and listens. You were in a hurry this morning. You walked past a snail."

"I did not see the snail," said Mai.

"The snail saw you," said the owl.

Then there was a third voice. It came from the trees behind them.

"Please," said the deer. "My little one is lost. She went towards the old gate and I cannot find her."

So the three of them walked together. Rusty smelled the way. The owl saw from the branch. And Mai listened very carefully to every small sound in the leaves.

They found the little fawn behind a fallen log, wet and shivering. The deer nosed her gently.

"Now," said the owl, "take this."

A leaf lay at Mai's feet. It was green and it glowed a little.

"Hold it when you walk home," said the owl. "Then the wood will walk with you."
examples: My name is Rusty. Thank you for helping me.
The wood only speaks to a person who stops and listens.
Take this leaf, then the wood will walk with you.
sections.heading: When the animals spoke

sections.body:
Mai did not know what to do at first. But she did things in the right order, and she did them slowly.

You can use these steps any time you find a small animal that is hurt or stuck.
examples: I am going to cut the thorns. Do not be afraid.
Easy. One thorn at a time.
I will stay here until you feel better.
sections.heading: How Mai helped the fox cub
steps: Look closely first. Find out what is stuck and what is scared.
Speak softly. Tell the animal what you are going to do.
Work slowly. One thorn at a time, never a fast pull.
Stop and check often. Give the animal a rest every few moments.
Free the leg gently, then let the animal move it.
Stay nearby for a little while. Sit down and keep it calm.

sections.body:
These are the new words in this story. Read them once, then read the story again and find them in the pictures of your mind.

A **cub** is a baby fox, a baby wolf or a baby bear. It is a small animal, and it cannot look after itself yet.

**Brambles** are thorny branches that grow together and grab hold of anything that touches them.

A **thicket** is a thick, tangled group of bushes. You cannot see far into a thicket.

To **listen** means to give your ears to a sound on purpose, and to wait. The forest in this story only answers people who listen.
sections.heading: The words of the Whispering Wood

terms.example: The cub sat down and shook the leaves off his fur.
terms.gloss: A baby fox, wolf or bear. A cub is small and still needs looking after.

terms.example: Rusty's leg was caught in the brambles.
terms.gloss: Thorny branches that grow together and hold on tightly to whatever touches them.

terms.example: A small voice came out of the thicket.
terms.gloss: A thick, tangled mass of bushes. You cannot see far into a thicket.

terms.example: Mai listened to every small sound in the leaves.
terms.gloss: To give your ears to a sound on purpose and wait for what comes next.

sections.body:
Mai walked home with the green leaf in her hand. The trees parted for her. The little lights came on in the dark under the branches, one by one, like a path of tiny stars.

When she came out of the wood, the fox cub was beside her. The old owl was on the wall of her grandmother's house. The deer and her fawn stood at the gate.

The lesson in this story is small and strange, and it is worth keeping. The world has more to say than we usually hear. But the saying is not for the busy ones. It is for the ones who stop, look closely, and stay a little longer.

Next time you walk past something small, try this. Stop. Look. Listen for one whole minute. You may be surprised what answers you.
examples: The world has more to say than we usually hear.
Stop. Look. Listen for one whole minute.
You may be surprised what answers you.
sections.heading: What Mai learned

item.summary: Mai hears a cry in the forest and finds a fox cub stuck in the brambles. Then the animals start to talk. You will meet the three parts of the story, learn four forest words, and find out why the forest only speaks to some people.
item.title: The Magical Forest of Talking Animals
